note: Claim records for the capitalism deep dive. status: drafted = written with sources linked; verified = an independent AI check confirmed the source supports the claim.

events.text: Luca Pacioli publishes the first widely read printed account of double-entry bookkeeping, a method Italian merchants and bankers had already used for generations. Firms still use it today.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Luca Pacioli (Wikipedia used because the Britannica page could not be opened; swap for a scholarly source when possible)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, Luca Pacioli (says Summa of 1494 is one of the first published descriptions of the Venetian method); Britannica URL could not be opened Corrected after this check: Britannica URL could not be opened. Wording softened: Pacioli described an existing method, and some sources call his the first, others one of the first, printed accounts.

events.text: The Atlantic slave trade carries about 12.5 million enslaved Africans onto ships; about 10.7 million survive the crossing, so close to 2 million die at sea. Their forced labor grows sugar, tobacco and cotton for world markets.

sources.cite: SlaveVoyages, Methodology of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade database

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened SlaveVoyages methodology essay (legacy site): 12.52 million departed, about 10.7 million disembarked, 1514–1866 Corrected after this check: Figures confirmed; original estimates-page URL could not be opened, so replaced with the SlaveVoyages page I opened. Added the deaths at sea plainly rather than leaving readers to subtract.

events.text: England charters the East India Company, a trading firm owned by shareholders that later rules much of India with its own army.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, East India Company (Wikipedia used because the Britannica page could not be opened; swap for a scholarly source when possible)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, East India Company: charter of 31 Dec 1600, joint-stock company, armies of about 260,000 at peak, ruled much of India until 1858 Corrected after this check: Text accurate; Britannica URL could not be opened, source replaced.

events.text: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) is founded. It sells shares that can be traded on the Amsterdam exchange, an early model of the modern company and stock market.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Dutch East India Company (Wikipedia used because the Britannica page could not be opened; swap for a scholarly source when possible)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, Dutch East India Company: founded 20 March 1602, shares traded in markets that became the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, one of the first joint-stock companies Corrected after this check: Text accurate; Britannica URL could not be opened, source replaced.

events.text: To control the nutmeg trade, VOC forces under Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquer the Banda Islands; most of the roughly 15,000 inhabitants are killed, enslaved or driven out.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands (cites Loth, Corn and Lape)
Cambridge World History of Genocide, Genocide in the Spice Islands

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands: pre-conquest population about 15,000; about 2,800 killed, 1,700 enslaved, 1,000 deported in 1621 under Coen; Lape estimates 90% killed, enslaved or deported. Cambridge chapter seen in search results only Corrected after this check: Text accurate; Britannica URL could not be opened, sources replaced. Conf Strong is right (population estimates are approximate).

events.text: Tulip bulb prices in the Dutch Republic soar and then collapse in early 1637. Historian Anne Goldgar found few bankruptcies and far less damage to the wider economy than the later legend claims.

sources.cite: Reviews in History (Institute of Historical Research), review of Goldgar, Tulipmania (2008)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Reviews in History review 666 of Goldgar’s Tulipmania: peak Feb 1637, collapse March 1637, few bankruptcies, legend based on a few pamphlets Corrected after this check: UChicago Press URL could not be opened; replaced with a scholarly review I opened. The modest-damage view is now the mainstream among historians of the episode, so Strong fits better than Contested.

events.text: The Bank of England is founded as a company owned by private investors, set up to lend money to King William III’s government for its war with France. Central banking grows out of arrangements like this.

sources.cite: Bank of England Museum, Why was the Bank of England founded?

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Bank of England Museum blog: Royal Charter 27 July 1694, raised £1.2 million from 1,268 investors for William III’s wars against France Corrected after this check: Original /about/history URL could not be opened; replaced. Clarified ownership (a joint-stock company of private investors, nationalised only in 1946) and which war.

events.text: The South Sea Bubble in Britain and the Mississippi Bubble in France burst after wild speculation in company shares, ruining many investors.

sources.cite: EBSCO Research Starters, Collapse of the South Sea Bubble

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened EBSCO Research Starters on the South Sea Bubble: share price from £128.5 to £1,000 and back to £135 by Sept 1720, thousands bankrupted; Mississippi scheme mentioned Corrected after this check: Text accurate; Britannica URL could not be opened, source replaced.

events.text: Over 5,000 Acts of Parliament enclose open fields and shared village land in England, turning them into private farms. Farm output rises, but many poor families lose rights to graze animals or gather fuel; historians still debate how far this pushed people into towns and factory work.

sources.cite: UK Parliament, Enclosing the land (same page opened on Parliament’s webtest mirror)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened UK Parliament Living Heritage, Enclosing the land (webtest.parliament.uk copy of the same path): over 5,200 enclosure bills 1604–1914, productivity gains, historians divided on whether it drove labourers off the land Corrected after this check: The record stated as fact that families moved to towns; Parliament’s own page says historians are divided on this. Rewrote so the migration effect is shown as debated, while keeping the loss of common rights.

events.text: After winning the Battle of Plassey (1757), the East India Company is granted the diwani, the right to collect Bengal’s land revenue, by the Mughal emperor in 1765. A trading company becomes a government.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757), Company rule in India (diwani of Bengal and Bihar granted 1765) and Treaty of Allahabad (granted by Shah Alam II) Corrected after this check: Facts correct; Britannica URL could not be opened. Added who granted the diwani (it followed the 1764 Battle of Buxar as well as Plassey).

events.text: Famine kills at least a million people in Bengal. The Company’s own 1770 estimate was a third of the population (about 10 million), while some modern historians put it near 1.2 million; they also debate how much Company tax collection and grain dealing worsened a drought-driven crisis.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Great Bengal famine of 1770 (summarizes Datta, Dyson, Roy)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, Great Bengal famine of 1770: Court of Directors 1770 estimate one-third (10 million), Datta about 1.2 million, Dyson calls 10 million barely credible; debate on drought vs Company policy Corrected after this check: ‘Kills millions’ overstated the lower end of modern estimates. Now gives the range, who made each estimate, and the causal debate.

events.text: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, arguing that the division of labor and free exchange make nations richer, while warning about monopolies and merchants who conspire against the public.

sources.cite: Online Library of Liberty, The Wealth of Nations

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Saw the Online Library of Liberty title page for the Cannan edition vol. 1 in search results (URL confirmed to exist); content checked from general knowledge of the text (Book I on division of labor; Book I ch. 10 on merchants conspiring)

events.text: The Industrial Revolution begins in Britain: machines, factories and coal-powered steam engines multiply output, first in cotton textiles. Historians still debate how quickly ordinary workers’ living standards rose in its early decades.

sources.cite: World History Encyclopedia, British Industrial Revolution

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened World History Encyclopedia, British Industrial Revolution: dated 1760–1840, cotton, coal, Watt engine, 2,500 steam engines by 1800 Corrected after this check: Britannica URL could not be opened, source replaced. Added the long-running ‘standard of living debate’ (optimists vs pessimists), which a fair historian on either side would mention.

events.text: Eli Whitney’s cotton gin makes it far cheaper to clean short-staple cotton, and slavery spreads rapidly across the US South to grow it.

sources.cite: National Archives, Eli Whitney’s patent for the cotton gin

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened National Archives, Eli Whitney’s Patent for the Cotton Gin (the record URL): patent 1794, inland sticky-seed cotton, growth of slavery called the most significant effect, slave states 6 to 15

events.text: About one million enslaved people in the United States are forcibly moved from the upper South to the cotton frontier, many sold away from their families.

sources.cite: Equal Justice Initiative, The Domestic Slave Trade
Smithsonian Magazine, Retracing Slavery’s Trail of Tears (2015)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened EJI, The Domestic Slave Trade (about one million moved 1810–1860; family separation) and Smithsonian, Retracing Slavery’s Trail of Tears (about a million in the 50 years before the Civil War); opened the EconPapers entry for Olmstead and Rhode 2018 Corrected after this check: Olmstead and Rhode (2018) is a critique of the ‘New History of Capitalism’ and does not support the one-million figure; Gilder Lehrman URL could not be opened. Replaced with two sources I opened and matched the dates they give (1810–1860).

events.text: David Ricardo explains comparative advantage: two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.

sources.cite: Online Library of Liberty, Ricardo, Principles

events.text: Britain’s Factory Act bans textile-mill work for children under nine, limits hours for older children, and creates the first factory inspectors.

sources.cite: The National Archives, 1833 Factory Act (education resource)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened The National Archives, 1833 Factory Act: no workers under nine, 9 hours for ages 9–13, 12 for 13–18, four inspectors, textiles; Parliament page exists (seen on webtest mirror)

events.text: Britain abolishes slavery in most of its colonies (not in Company-ruled India) and pays £20 million, about 40% of that year’s government spending, to slave owners. The enslaved get nothing and are forced into years of unpaid “apprenticeship” until 1838.

sources.cite: UCL Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery
Full Fact, What we know about the government loan to pay slave owners (2018)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Full Fact on the Slavery Abolition Act loan: £20 million to owners, about 40% of spending, exceptions such as India, unpaid apprenticeship, no compensation for the freed. UCL LBS page could not be opened Corrected after this check: Facts right; added the scale of the payment and the India exception, and a source I could open alongside UCL.

events.text: About a million people die in the Irish famine and over a million emigrate. Food exports from Ireland continue, and historians debate how far the British government’s free-market relief policy deepened the disaster.

sources.cite: UK Parliament, The Great Famine (Parliament and Ireland)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened UK Parliament Living Heritage, The Great Famine (webtest mirror): 1845–1852, about 1,000,000 deaths, Trevelyan limited aid on laissez-faire principles, food exports continued Corrected after this check: Text accurate and fairly balanced; Britannica URL could not be opened, source replaced (this is Parliament’s own page, served from its webtest host; the www.parliament.uk path is very likely the same).

events.text: Britain repeals the Corn Laws, which had protected landowners with grain tariffs, a turning point toward free trade.

sources.cite: EBSCO Research Starters, British Parliament Repeals the Corn Laws

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened EBSCO Research Starters, British Parliament Repeals the Corn Laws: grain tariffs kept prices high for landowners; 1846 repeal under Peel was the first step to free trade Corrected after this check: Text accurate; original Parliament URL could not be opened, source replaced.

events.text: Marx and Engels publish The Communist Manifesto, one of the most influential critiques of capitalism ever written (see the Marxism–Leninism deep dive).

sources.cite: Marxists Internet Archive, Manifesto of the Communist Party

events.text: British laws of 1855–1862 let ordinary companies offer limited liability: investors can lose only what they put in. This makes it easier to raise money from many small shareholders, though critics then and now warn it lets owners push losses onto creditors.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Wikipedia, Limited Liability Act 1855 and Limited liability: 1855 act first general grant (more than 25 members), 1856 Act cut to seven members, 1862 Act extended to insurers Corrected after this check: Facts right; Britannica URL could not be opened. Added the standard objection (moral hazard) so both sides appear.

events.text: Japan’s Meiji Restoration begins state-led industrialization: the government builds model factories, mines, railways and shipyards. In the 1880s it sells most of its factories and mines, often cheaply, to investors with close government ties, and some grow into the zaibatsu.

sources.cite: Britannica, Empire of Japan: The emergence of modern Japan
Shippensburg University course page, Meiji Economic Development

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Opened Britannica, Empire of Japan: The emergence of modern Japan (pilot factories sold in the 1880s to investors close to officials, who became the zaibatsu) and a Shippensburg course page (railways later nationalized in 1907, Mitsubishi got Nagasaki shipyard 1883, Mitsui got Miike mine 1888) Corrected after this check: Railways and banks were not generally sold to the zaibatsu (main railways were nationalized in 1906–07). Corrected what was sold and added the political-connections point.

events.text: During the era of the classical gold standard, with steamships, railways and telegraphs cutting costs, world trade and cross-border investment rise to levels not seen again until the late 20th century. This ‘first globalization’ also coincides with the height of European empire.

A financial panic in Vienna (May 1873) and New York (September 1873) starts a long period of falling prices and slow growth in Europe and North America, later called the Long Depression; historians debate how deep it really was.

In the Congo Free State, owned personally by King Leopold II of Belgium, forced rubber collection enforced by hostage-taking, mutilation and killing causes mass death. Because no census was taken, estimates of the toll range widely, from about 1 million to 10 million or more.
The US Sherman Antitrust Act outlaws agreements that restrain trade, such as cartels, and attempts to monopolize a market.
Max Weber’s The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism argues that religious ideas about work and saving helped shape modern capitalism. The thesis is still debated.
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York kills 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women, behind locked doors. It leads to new safety and labor laws.

sources.cite: Cornell ILR, The Triangle Factory Fire

events.text: Ford introduces the moving assembly line (1913) and then the five-dollar day (1914), cutting the price of a car and roughly doubling usual factory pay. The high wage was partly meant to stop workers quitting the fast, repetitive line, and to qualify, workers had to meet company rules on their home lives.

sources.cite: The Henry Ford, Moving assembly line

events.text: The US creates the Federal Reserve after repeated bank panics.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, Federal Reserve Act

events.text: Arthur Pigou’s Economics of Welfare explains what are now called externalities, costs such as pollution that fall on people outside a deal, and proposes taxing them.
After the Wall Street crash of October 1929, US output collapses and unemployment rises from about 3% to about 25% in 1933. Thousands of banks fail.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, The Great Depression

events.text: The US Smoot–Hawley Tariff raises import duties; other countries retaliate and world trade shrinks. Economists still debate how much it deepened the Depression.

sources.cite: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

events.text: Drought and years of plowing up native grassland for wheat bring the Dust Bowl to the southern Great Plains, driving hundreds of thousands of people off the land.

sources.cite: Library of Congress, Dust Bowl migration

events.text: Roosevelt’s New Deal adds bank deposit insurance, the separation of commercial and investment banking (Glass–Steagall), Social Security, minimum wages and the legal right to join a union. Supporters credit it with stability; critics argue some policies slowed recovery, and many farm and domestic workers, often Black, were left out at first.
Keynes’s General Theory argues that economies can stay stuck with high unemployment and that government spending can lift demand.
Ronald Coase asks why firms exist at all, and answers that markets have costs (finding partners, making contracts), so some work is cheaper to organize inside a company.

Joseph Schumpeter describes “creative destruction”: new firms and technologies destroy old ones. He also predicted that capitalism would slowly give way to socialism, not because it failed but because its success would weaken the institutions and attitudes that support it.
Two rival classics appear: Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom warns that central planning leads to tyranny, and Polanyi’s The Great Transformation argues that unregulated markets tear societies apart.
At Bretton Woods, 44 Allied nations set up the IMF and the World Bank and a system of fixed exchange rates tied to the US dollar and gold.

sources.cite: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

events.text: West Germany’s 1948 currency reform, organized by the Western Allies, and Ludwig Erhard’s lifting of most price controls start the “social market economy”, combining competitive markets with social insurance and, later, a strong role for unions. Rapid growth (the “economic miracle”) follows; economists debate how much came from the reforms and how much from postwar rebuilding and Marshall aid.

Swedish union economists Gösta Rehn and Rudolf Meidner propose the model behind Sweden’s system: equal pay for equal work across firms, active job retraining and a large welfare state alongside private ownership.

Under Park Chung-hee, who took power in a 1961 military coup and ruled until 1979, South Korea grows rapidly through state-directed, export-led industrialization: cheap credit for chosen firms (the chaebol), strict export targets, and suppressed labor unions. Incomes rise fast, while political opponents are jailed.
Milton Friedman’s New York Times essay argues that a company’s social responsibility is to increase its profits within the rules of the game.
President Nixon ends the dollar’s convertibility into gold (August 1971), and by 1973 the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates has collapsed.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, Nixon ends convertibility

events.text: Two oil shocks and “stagflation” (high inflation with high unemployment) undermine faith in Keynesian management and open the way for market-oriented reforms.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, The Great Inflation

events.text: After the 1973 military coup in Chile, economists trained in Chicago (the “Chicago Boys”) privatize, cut tariffs and create private pensions; there was a deep crash in 1982, and fast growth and big falls in poverty came mainly from the late 1980s and after democracy returned in 1990. The dictatorship killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and tortured tens of thousands.

sources.cite: Cato Journal, The Fall of Chile (2020)
Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos (Chile)

events.text: China begins “reform and opening up”: farm families may sell surplus crops, special economic zones welcome foreign firms, and markets slowly spread under Communist Party rule. Over the next four decades, by World Bank figures, about 800 million people in China leave extreme poverty.
Britain under Margaret Thatcher and the US under Ronald Reagan cut top tax rates, curb union power and (in Britain) privatize state industries.
Economist John Williamson names the “Washington Consensus”: ten market-oriented policies promoted by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury.

sources.cite: Peterson Institute, What Washington Means by Policy Reform

events.text: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis, India’s Finance Minister Manmohan Singh abolishes most industrial licensing, cuts tariffs and opens to foreign investment.

Russia’s rapid transition (“shock therapy”, voucher privatization, the 1995 loans-for-shares deals that created billionaire oligarchs) coincides with a deep slump, a 1998 default and a sharp fall in male life expectancy. Causes of the death spike are debated.

sources.cite: Brainerd & Cutler, Journal of Economic Perspectives (2005)

events.text: The Asian financial crisis hits Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea when a rush of short-term foreign money reverses, exposing fixed currency pegs and weak banks. Economists still argue over the blame: footloose capital and IMF austerity, or crony lending and poor regulation.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, Asian financial crisis

events.text: China joins the World Trade Organization. Research later finds that the surge of Chinese imports, which accelerated after it joined, explains about a quarter of the fall in US manufacturing jobs from 1990 to 2007, with lasting damage in hard-hit towns, while lowering prices for consumers.

sources.cite: Autor, Dorn & Hanson, American Economic Review (2013)

events.text: The US housing bubble bursts; Lehman Brothers fails on 15 September 2008 and a global financial crisis follows. The official US inquiry (2011) concluded the crisis was avoidable, but its members split over the causes.

The Rana Plaza garment factory building collapses in Bangladesh, killing more than 1,130 workers who made clothes for global brands and injuring over 2,500. It leads to a binding safety accord between brands and unions.

sources.cite: International Labour Organization, The Rana Plaza accident and its aftermath

events.text: Thomas Piketty’s Capital in the Twenty-First Century argues that wealth tends to concentrate when returns on capital outpace growth. Other economists dispute the data and the theory.

sources.cite: Harvard University Press, Capital in the Twenty-First Century

events.text: The US Business Roundtable says companies should serve customers, workers, suppliers and communities as well as shareholders, a shift away from the Friedman view. Some critics doubt behavior changed; others warn that managers answerable to everyone are answerable to no one.

sources.cite: Business Roundtable, Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation

events.text: A sharp scholarly dispute: Sullivan and Hickel argue that the rise of capitalism made welfare worse for centuries; Rutar and others reply that poverty was common before capitalism and that colonialism is not the same thing as capitalism.
The World Bank raises its extreme-poverty line to $3.00 a day. By that measure roughly 800 million people remain extremely poor, compared with about 2 billion or more in 1990.

sources.cite: World Bank, June 2025 update to global poverty lines

events.text: The World Inequality Report 2026 estimates that the richest 10% own about three-quarters of the world’s wealth and the poorest half about 2%.
The economics Nobel goes to Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson for research on how institutions shaped by colonization explain why some nations are richer than others.
The economics Nobel goes to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for explaining growth driven by innovation and creative destruction.
US government data show that about one in five new business establishments closes within its first year and about half within five years.

sources.cite: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, The Economics Daily

people.name: Ibn Khaldun
people.text: Argued in the Muqaddimah that high taxes eventually shrink the economy and that labor creates value, ideas later economists rediscovered.

people.name: Adam Smith
people.text: Explained the division of labor and used the image of an “invisible hand” for how self-interest can serve others in markets, but also attacked monopolies and argued that no society can flourish when most of its members are poor.

people.name: David Ricardo
people.text: Showed how countries gain from trade through comparative advantage; a successful stockbroker and member of Parliament.

people.name: John Stuart Mill
people.text: Defended free markets and liberty but supported worker cooperatives, inheritance taxes and women’s rights.

people.name: Karl Marx
people.text: The most influential critic of capitalism; argued that profit comes from labor that workers are not paid for, and that capitalism’s recurring crises would lead workers to overthrow it.

people.name: Andrew Carnegie
people.text: Built a steel empire through relentless cost-cutting and fought unions (his company broke the 1892 Homestead strike, in which workers and Pinkerton guards were killed), then gave away most of his fortune, especially to libraries and universities.

people.name: Mary Harris Jones (“Mother Jones”)
people.text: Labor organizer for miners and child workers; the nickname came from the workers she organized, who called her “mother”.

people.name: Max Weber
people.text: Linked the spirit of capitalism to Protestant ideas about work and saving, and studied bureaucracy and the modern state.

people.name: Henry Ford
people.text: Made cars affordable with the moving assembly line and high wages; also published antisemitic propaganda in his newspaper.

people.name: Frances Perkins
people.text: First woman in a US cabinet; as Labor Secretary she shaped Social Security, the minimum wage and limits on child labor.

sources.cite: US Department of Labor, Frances Perkins

people.name: John Maynard Keynes
people.text: Argued that governments must manage demand to avoid mass unemployment; helped design the Bretton Woods system.

people.name: Joseph Schumpeter
people.text: Described entrepreneurs and “creative destruction” as the engine of capitalism.

people.name: Karl Polanyi
people.region: Austria-Hungary, Britain, the United States and Canada
people.text: Argued that turning land, labor and money into market goods provokes society to protect itself.

people.name: Friedrich Hayek
people.region: Austria, Britain, the United States and Germany
people.text: Argued that prices carry knowledge no planner could gather; Nobel Prize 1974.

people.name: Raúl Prebisch
people.text: Argued that poorer countries exporting raw materials lose out in trade with industrial countries, inspiring import-substitution policies across Latin America.

people.name: Ludwig Erhard
people.text: Launched West Germany’s social market economy in 1948 and later became chancellor.

people.name: Milton Friedman
people.text: Argued for free markets and steady money growth; Nobel Prize 1976. Chilean economists trained in Chicago advised the Pinochet dictatorship, and his 1975 meeting with Pinochet drew lasting criticism; he replied that he gave similar advice to communist governments.

people.name: Ronald Coase
people.text: Explained why firms exist and how property rights can settle conflicts like pollution; Nobel Prize 1991.

people.name: Park Chung-hee
people.text: Military ruler who drove export-led industrialization while repressing opposition and unions.

people.name: Deng Xiaoping
people.text: Led China’s market reforms after 1978 while keeping one-party rule; ordered the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown.

people.name: Elinor Ostrom
people.text: Showed that communities often manage shared resources well without either state control or privatization; Nobel Prize 2009.

people.name: Amartya Sen
people.region: India, Britain and the United States
people.text: Showed that famines come from people losing the means to buy food, not only from shortage; Nobel Prize 1998.

people.name: Muhammad Yunus
people.text: Founded Grameen Bank to make small loans to poor borrowers, mostly women; Nobel Peace Prize 2006. The results of microcredit are debated.

people.name: Manmohan Singh
people.text: As finance minister in 1991 he opened India’s economy; later prime minister from 2004 to 2014.

people.name: Walter Rodney
people.text: Argued in How Europe Underdeveloped Africa that colonial capitalism drained Africa’s wealth; assassinated in Guyana in 1980.

people.name: Hernando de Soto
people.text: Argued that the poor hold vast assets they cannot use as capital because they lack legal property titles.

people.name: Deirdre McCloskey
people.text: Argues that the great enrichment came mostly from new respect for ordinary business people and innovation, not from trade or exploitation.

people.name: Ha-Joon Chang
people.text: Argues that rich countries grew rich using protection and state support, then told poorer countries not to.

sources.cite: SOAS University of London, Ha-Joon Chang

people.name: Thomas Piketty
people.text: Built long-run data on income and wealth inequality and argues for global wealth taxes.

sources.cite: Paris School of Economics, Thomas Piketty
